title: Getting started with ChatGPT
description: A direct introduction to using ChatGPT, with a route into OpenAI’s AI Foundations course. A sensible first stop before chasing advanced techniques.
bestFor: Your first conversations with ChatGPT
needs: No programming required.

title: Elements of AI
description: An introduction to what AI is, what it can do, and how to think about its effects. A useful foundation before focusing on a particular tool.
bestFor: Understanding AI beyond a single product
needs: An account is required for complete course access. Six chapters with exercises; check the course FAQ for completion requirements.

title: Wharton Prompt Library
description: Reusable prompts with guidance for testing and adapting them. Includes an idea-challenging “Devil’s Advocate” example and a practical checklist for evaluating outputs.
bestFor: Improving a prompt you actually use
needs: Test prompts with your own tasks and model. Reusing the library’s prompts requires attribution to Ethan and Lilach Mollick under CC BY 4.0.

title: Google AI Essentials
description: Hands-on practice in prompting, workplace tasks, and responsible use. A structured option for people who want a short course with a completion certificate.
credential: Google completion certificate; not a professional license.
needs: No technical experience required. Subscription pricing varies by country and enrollment platform.
bestFor: A structured introduction to AI at work

title: AI concepts for developers and technology professionals
description: A beginner learning path with seven modules covering core AI concepts, generative AI and agents, language, speech, vision, information extraction, and retrieval-augmented generation. Assumes basic computing and math knowledge.
bestFor: Technical beginners who want a guided AI overview
needs: Basic computing and math knowledge; aimed at developers and AI engineers.

title: Generative AI for Beginners
description: A 21-lesson curriculum with Python and JavaScript examples: chat, search, images, retrieval, agents, and application security.
needs: Programming fundamentals. Some exercises require model accounts, API usage, or local setup.
bestFor: Building a foundation through working examples

title: OpenAI Cookbook
description: Practical examples and guides for building with the OpenAI API. Start with a use case and work through the accompanying code.
bestFor: Finding an implementation pattern
needs: Coding experience and any model access required by the selected example.

title: AI Agents Course
description: Learn agent concepts, work with established frameworks, and build an evaluated final project. Includes retrieval, observability, and a game-playing example.
needs: Basic Python and LLM knowledge; a Hugging Face account for publishing projects.
credential: Free course certificates: a fundamentals certificate after Unit 1, and a completion certificate after the required use case and final challenge.
bestFor: Moving from chat prompts to working agents

title: Hugging Face Learn
description: Courses on language models, agents, context engineering, audio, and other practical topics in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Check each course for prerequisites.
bestFor: Exploring additional technical subjects

title: Make repeated API context cost less
description: Learn how shared prompt prefixes, stable tool definitions and cache breakpoints affect reuse. Includes diagnostics for misses; compare cache-write costs with the savings from repeated reads.
needs: An API integration with repeated context. Rates and cache behavior vary by model; a persistent session does not guarantee a cache hit.
bestFor: Reducing avoidable latency and input costs

title: Gemini Notebook / NotebookLM
description: Work with a collection of documents and ask questions tied to those sources. Useful for comparing readings and tracing a summary back to the underlying material.
needs: Google account. Drive sources sync automatically; check other imported sources for freshness and verify citations against originals.
bestFor: Reading a stack of sources

title: Zotero
description: Collect, annotate, organize, and cite original research. A useful companion to AI reading tools when you need a durable source library.
needs: Desktop app or browser connector. This is a reference manager, not a generative AI model.
bestFor: Keeping the evidence behind your work

title: n8n
description: Connect apps, triggers, and model calls in a visual workflow. Useful when an AI step needs to sit inside a repeatable business process.
cost: Paid cloud by workflow execution · self-host options
needs: App credentials and some workflow setup. Account for model calls and hosting separately; review license terms before reselling.
bestFor: Connecting AI to the apps you use

title: LM Studio
description: Explore open models on your own computer through a desktop interface. Its Bionic agent also supports document and coding work.
needs: Hardware requirements depend on the model. Local inference is free; optional cloud plans and web tools can send data off your device. Check which mode you are using.
bestFor: Experimenting with local models

title: ChatGPT Ads for Shopify
description: A product-catalog integration for creating and measuring paid ChatGPT campaigns. Review the listing’s data permissions and current availability before connecting a store. A marketing channel, not evidence of earnings.
bestFor: Merchants evaluating a new advertising channel
needs: A Shopify store; check access, data permissions, and campaign costs.

title: AI Town
description: A virtual village where AI characters talk and socialize. An open-source starting point for experimenting with simulated worlds; supports several model providers, including OpenAI-compatible APIs.
imageAlt: Editorial pixel illustration of a small village among green trees
bestFor: Exploring playful agent simulations
needs: JavaScript/TypeScript development setup, Convex (cloud or self-hosted), and a model provider. Supports local Ollama; the README includes Docker and Windows setup paths.

title: A document summarization workflow
description: An inspectable template collection for summarizing URLs, text, and PDFs. Adapt one input path first, then compare its summaries with the original documents.
needs: n8n, model credentials, and optional OCR credentials. Review webhook access and every destination before using private files.
bestFor: Turning a repetitive reading task into a workflow

title: Build a demo with Gradio
description: Turn a Python function or model into a small web interface. The README includes a minimal working example and options for sharing a demo.
needs: Python 3.10 or later. Model and hosting costs vary. Enabling share=True creates a public URL even when computation runs on your computer; review access before sharing.
bestFor: Making an experiment usable by someone else

title: Realtime Console
description: An example for exploring the Realtime API with WebRTC, event logging and client-side function calls. A useful reference for understanding voice interactions.
bestFor: Understanding realtime events and voice interactions
needs: Node.js and an OpenAI API key. Last repository push: August 2025; check current model availability and dependencies before running it. Not tested by this site.

title: Realtime voice agents
description: A Next.js demo of voice agents that call tools and hand work to specialists. Compare the chat-supervisor and sequential-handoff patterns.
needs: Node.js, TypeScript familiarity, and an OpenAI API key. Not archived; last repository push January 2026. Examples reference older models, so check availability, costs and safeguards before adapting. We have not run this demo.
bestFor: Prototyping a voice interface

title: Hugging Face Spaces
description: A directory of working AI demos across text, images, audio, and code. Individual projects vary in quality, maintenance, and data handling; inclusion is a discovery link, not an endorsement.
bestFor: Discovering and trying community experiments

title: Make Real
description: A sketch-to-interface project built with the tldraw SDK. The repository was archived on February 20, 2026; treat it as a reference rather than an actively maintained starter. Its README links to a separate starter repository.
imageAlt: Editorial pixel illustration of sketches turning into an interface
bestFor: Studying a sketch-to-interface experiment
needs: Archived reference; use the README’s separate starter link for follow-up research.

title: Test the business before you build
description: Market research, business-plan examples, startup costs, and break-even planning in one reference. Use it to define a customer and a deliverable before investing in an AI service.
bestFor: Validating a service or product idea

title: Choosing a pricing model
description: Compare subscriptions, usage-based billing, tiers, and hybrid models. Useful for a software product whose model and support costs change with customer usage.
bestFor: Pricing an AI software product
needs: Commercial guidance from a payments provider; adapt the examples to your own costs and customer research.

title: Fyxer: an assistant business
description: A vendor case study on splitting email assistance into smaller jobs, testing drafts against real tasks, and using edits as feedback. Useful product-design lessons; retention and revenue figures are company-reported.
bestFor: Studying a focused subscription product

title: Harvey: software for a specific profession
description: A September 2026 case study of legal drafting with source context and lawyers’ preferences. Read it for how a specialist product organizes documents and review; the claimed improvements are reported by the vendor.
bestFor: Understanding a vertical software business
needs: Vendor account, not independently audited business results. Professional applications require appropriate expertise and review.

title: Stanford AI Index
description: Annual evidence on AI adoption, investment, and broader trends. Useful market context for a business idea; aggregate indicators are not proof that a particular service will sell.
bestFor: Checking a market story against broader evidence

title: International AI Safety Report 2026
description: A scientific synthesis of general-purpose AI capabilities, emerging risks, and risk management. Its authors distinguish evidence from uncertainty; the report does not endorse a particular policy.

safety.why: A broad scientific synthesis is a useful foundation before reading individual claims about AI risk.
safety.readFirst: Start with the executive summary, then follow the chapter behind a claim.
safety.limits: Evidence is uneven across risks; a synthesis is not a prediction that every scenario will occur.

title: AI Incident Database
description: A searchable index of reported real-world AI harms and near harms. Follow the underlying sources for context and the status of individual claims; an indexed report is not a final finding.

safety.why: Connects abstract debates to reported harms and the sources behind them.
safety.readFirst: Search for a use case you recognize and open the underlying reports.
safety.limits: An indexed incident is not a final finding, and report counts do not measure the prevalence of harm.

title: AI Risk Management Framework
description: Voluntary guidance for managing AI risks across the life of a system, with links to a companion Playbook and generative AI profile. NIST notes that version 1.0 is being revised.

safety.why: A practical framework for assigning responsibility and reviewing risks across an AI system’s life.
safety.readFirst: Use the companion Playbook to turn a risk discussion into specific actions.
safety.limits: Voluntary guidance, not certification or proof that a system is safe. Version 1.0 is being revised.

title: AI Now Institute
description: Research and policy advocacy examining AI companies, concentrated power, and public accountability.

safety.why: Examines who holds power, who bears costs, and how public institutions could respond.
safety.readFirst: Start with the landscape report, then explore a policy topic that affects you.
safety.limits: Research and advocacy from an organization with a stated policy agenda; examine the evidence behind each proposal.

title: PauseAI
description: The case for pausing development of the most powerful AI systems, alongside policy proposals and ways to get involved. This is an advocacy organization.

safety.why: A direct source for the argument to pause the development of the most powerful AI systems.
safety.readFirst: Read the proposal and its scope before deciding whether to support a campaign.
safety.limits: An advocacy position. Its claims and proposed remedies should be assessed separately.

title: METR evaluations
description: Research on autonomous capabilities, evaluation reliability, and developer productivity. Read the methods and limits of each study. METR discloses lab partnerships and model access.

safety.why: Empirical evaluations help distinguish measured capabilities from claims about what agents can do.
safety.readFirst: Start with an evaluation’s tasks, access and limitations. The September 2026 Opus 5.5 assessment covers AI-research capabilities, not an alignment verdict.
safety.limits: Lab tasks may not generalize to everyday work. Check disclosed relationships and model access.

title: Apollo Research
description: Technical work on model deception, scheming, and alignment evaluations. Study findings describe tested conditions; they do not establish the prevalence of a behavior in everyday use.

safety.why: Studies model deception and behavior that standard usefulness benchmarks can miss.
safety.readFirst: Compare the scheming studies with the system-card evaluation summaries. Check whether models recognized the tests and what the baselines were.
safety.limits: Behavior elicited in an evaluation does not establish how frequently it happens in deployment.

title: AI Security Institute
provider: UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
description: Government research on advanced AI capabilities, public safety, and risk mitigations, alongside evaluation tools and technical reports.

safety.why: Offers government-led evaluations and research on advanced AI capabilities and safeguards.
safety.readFirst: Compare a capability study’s tasks, model access and limits. The open-weight cyber analysis distinguishes short tasks from longer simulated networks; those ranges lack some real-world defenses.
safety.limits: A UK government perspective. Evaluation results depend on access, methods, and the systems tested.

title: MIT AI Risk Repository
description: A structured collection of AI risks and the frameworks that describe them. Useful for checking whether a discussion overlooks social, security, or system-level harms.

safety.why: A map of risk categories helps reveal what a narrow discussion leaves out.
safety.readFirst: Start with the risk repository, then use the Risk Navigator to connect risk categories with incidents and governance records.
safety.limits: A catalog organizes risks; it does not establish that every risk is equally likely or severe.

title: Epoch AI
description: Data explorers and research on model capabilities, compute, and AI infrastructure. Check measurement methods, coverage, and assumptions before comparing claims.

safety.why: Makes claims about capabilities and compute easier to inspect against underlying measurements.
safety.readFirst: Open a data explorer and read its definitions before comparing models or trends.
safety.limits: Benchmarks and compute estimates have assumptions; projections are not observations.

title: Privacy considerations with AI tools
description: A readable guide to what happens to your data in AI apps, integrations, and local or cloud tools. Covers privacy settings, retention, and the limits of “private” modes.

safety.why: Helps you make a concrete decision about what information to share with an AI tool.
safety.readFirst: Start by auditing extensions and connected apps, then check privacy settings and retention. Revoke access you no longer want.
safety.limits: Advice from a digital-rights organization. Product settings change; follow its links to current provider documentation.

title: AI and cyber security: what you need to know
description: A nontechnical introduction to AI security for managers: unreliable outputs, attacks on AI systems, sensitive data, and responsibility within an organization.

safety.why: Gives people responsible for adopting AI a way to discuss security with their teams.
safety.readFirst: Read the sections on cyber risks and what leaders can do, then use the questions for managers to review your own organization.
safety.limits: A security overview, not a complete treatment of social risks; some product examples reflect an earlier generation of tools.

title: Measure whether AI is paying off
description: A practical approach to comparing AI use with delivery time, quality and business outcomes. Includes review and correction time, setup and support costs; its ROI example is illustrative, not a measured earnings result.
needs: Useful for team leads and service providers. The product walkthrough uses ChatGPT administrator analytics; verify access in your plan.
bestFor: Evaluating a workflow before expanding it
